slides.notes: Begin by treating the introduction as a method lecture, not a preface. The source span is short, but the notebook converts it into a working rule for Geometry I: every definition should eventually meet a figure, a perturbation, and a check that students can inspect.

Emphasize the division of labor between the scanned source, the notebook, and the deck. The source orients the topic and page span; the notebook supplies original prose and artifacts; the lecture adds instructor pacing so students see why the visual contract matters.

Name the four roles before giving examples. Data records the object, an operation changes the object or its description, an invariant states what should survive, and a check makes the survival auditable. This vocabulary will return throughout affine, projective, Euclidean, and convex geometry.

Use the three questions as a live reading protocol. Ask students to point to the acted-on object, then identify the permitted change, then name the relation that should remain stable. The diagram matters only because it lets those answers be inspected.

Slow down on the coordinate warning. Coordinates are powerful because they make measurement executable, but they are a chosen language for the geometry. The table separates point, chart, transformation, and invariant so students can diagnose when a calculation is chart-dependent.

Frame examples as stress tests rather than warmups. A small triangle, four collinear points, or a finite sample can expose the role of a definition, produce a counterexample, or suggest an invariant. The general theorem then has a visible target.

Connect the two notebook figures to the lecture contract. The loop names the study rhythm, while the measurement figure models how examples generate an invariant candidate. The point is not decorative output; it is an auditable visual experiment stored in the artifact tree.

Present the certificate as the quiet engineering layer behind the mathematics. Image size and pixel variation only prove that a visual exists and is nonblank, while geometry checks record the claimed invariant. Together they make the notebook inspectable by people and scripts.

Treat the pitfalls as mathematical failure modes. A drawing can seduce without proving, a coordinate system can hide the object, and a numerical pattern can be mistaken for a theorem. The cure is to label assumptions and decide what would fail.

Turn the applied lab into a reusable template. Before proving a later definition, students choose an object, perturb one input, predict an invariant, and write a small check. This gives even abstract topics a concrete first experiment.

Use the course map to show why the introduction matters. Group actions, affine structure, projective charts, Euclidean measurements, and convex sets look different, but each lesson can be read through the same object, operation, invariant, and check pattern.

Close by making the habit portable. A learner should leave the introduction able to ask what is represented, what is allowed to change, what relation survives, and what evidence has been recorded. That habit is the through-line for Geometry I.
